title: The Revenge Tragedy and the Hesitating Prince
welcome_lead: Open Shakespeare's c.1600 tragedy and examine how he transforms the revenge genre into a meditation on consciousness itself.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on Shakespeare's Hamlet: revenge tragedy, soliloquy, and the hesitating tragic hero.
final_note: Hamlet's tragedy is not that he delays — it is that he cannot stop thinking about delaying.

walkthroughs.body_html: Shakespeare's Hamlet (c.1600) reworks Kyd's The Spanish Tragedy and an earlier lost 'Ur-Hamlet'. The conventions are present — ghost demanding vengeance, delay, madness, play-within-play, multiple corpses — but Shakespeare interiorises them. Where Hieronimo rages publicly, Hamlet meditates. Critics including G.K. Hunter argue the genre's external machinery becomes psychological in Shakespeare's hands.

The third-act soliloquy (3.1) is not strictly about suicide: 'To be' is existence itself, 'not to be' its negation. The speech is structured as syllogism, with Hamlet weighing the unknown of death against the known of suffering. Critics from A.C. Bradley to Stephen Greenblatt note its philosophical detachment — Hamlet speaks as if of someone else, exemplifying his characteristic self-alienation.

Hamlet survives in three early texts: Q1 (1603, around 2,200 lines, often called the 'bad quarto', possibly reconstructed from memory), Q2 (1604/5, around 3,800 lines, probably from Shakespeare's papers), and F1 (1623, with cuts and additions). The famous 'How all occasions' soliloquy appears only in Q2. Modern editions are composites; the 'authentic' Hamlet does not exist.

A soliloquy is when characters argue with each other.
